name: Erik Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Erik. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a construction crew, so we build new lines rather than fix old ones. Right now we're running a new feeder, that's a main line, out to a solar farm off the old quarry road, eleven kilometres of poles and wire. A normal day is setting poles with the digger-derrick, framing the cross-arms, then pulling wire with the tensioner, and I've usually got two apprentices with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching the apprentices. I came up through an apprenticeship myself, and old Harold took me under his wing, so I try to do the same. What wears me out is the travel and the early starts. Some months we're an hour out each way, and I miss Sofia's school things. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check a clearance rule or settle an argument in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, like a lot of things. People wanted it to do our jobs, and it turns out you still need a man with a spanner. I'd say that at the depot and at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. The apprentices have a future, I keep building, we keep paying down the house. We're ahead on the mortgage and we've got a good bit saved, so we're steady either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep training the lads. Keep overpaying the mortgage a bit, we want it gone by the time Daniel's at college. I'd keep using the phone AI for the odd question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you tell me about an argument the AI settled in the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the lads were arguing about how close you can run a line to a barn roof. I said one number, Kyle said another. Asked the phone, it gave the rule and where it came from. I was right. Kyle bought the coffees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be disappointed in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people selling it, I suppose. And maybe some of the young ones who hoped they'd never have to climb. But honestly, a man who's afraid of climbing should find another trade.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold and you still need a person with a spanner, which I'd say at the depot and the football club.
S0.think: I'd be pleased because the apprentices would have a future and I'd keep building. We're ahead on the mortgage with good savings, so we're steady either way.
S0.do: Carries on training apprentices and overpaying the mortgage, aiming to clear it before his son starts college. Keeps using the AI on his phone for the odd question.
S0.quote: Asked the phone, it gave the rule and where it came from. I was right. Kyle bought the coffees.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is grounded and secure, and his main pride is training apprentices as he was trained. He uses AI lightly and practically. His remark about people afraid of climbing shows a firm, old-school view of the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how business works, better tools come along and you learn them. Nobody's owed a job, but a good worker will always find one. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new kit as well as the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think construction crews will be the last to feel it. You can't send a drone to set a pole in a bog. But I'd worry about the apprenticeship numbers, if the company decides it needs fewer new people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of other crews had tried the new survey drones and planning software, I'd learn them properly. I'd make sure my apprentices learned them too. Keep saving, keep overpaying, no big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit of worry for the lads coming up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody's owed a job. Would you say that to Kyle if his apprenticeship got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd say it about the world, not to his face. To his face I'd say, I'll ring round, and I would. There's three contractors near here who'd take a good apprentice. That's what you do for your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fifteen and wants to do something with computers. I'd say fine, but get your hands dirty too. Do a summer with me on the crew. A man should know how the lights get to his house.

S1.say: I'd say this is how business works, better tools come and you learn them, nobody is owed a job but good workers find one, and apprentices should learn the new and old kit.
S1.think: Construction crews will feel it last, because you can't send a drone to set a pole in a bog. My worry is the company cutting apprenticeship numbers.
S1.do: Learns survey drones and planning software properly once other crews have tested them, and makes sure his apprentices learn them too. Keeps saving and overpaying the mortgage without big changes.
S1.feel: Calm, with some worry for the young workers coming up.
S1.quote: I'd say it about the world, not to his face. To his face I'd say, I'll ring round, and I would.
S1.fieldNote: When gently pressed, his tough public line gave way to personal loyalty toward his apprentice. He waits for proof before learning new tools but then learns them properly. He wants his son to have hands-on experience whatever he studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and that's the companies' fault for rushing, not the technology's. I'm all for business, but you don't throw a whole country's workers out in two years. I'd say families need to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. If robots can build lines by 2028, my trade's finished before Daniel's out of school. We've got savings and the house is two-thirds paid, but two years doesn't give the apprentices anywhere to go, or me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop the extension we'd planned for the back of the house and put that money on the mortgage. I'd sit down with Rosa and work out how long we last on her bookkeeping and our savings. I'd tell Daniel to rethink his college plans, maybe a trade that robots would take longer to reach. And I'd sell firewood off our bit of woodland for some extra coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked. But I'd be quiet at dinner, and Rosa would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't know. That's the hard part. I'm supposed to be the one who knows. I'd tell them to save every penny and stick together, and I'd keep ringing round, but I wouldn't lie to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should pull together rather than look to government. What if that's not enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the help, if it was there. I'd not like it. But I won't let my kids go short for my pride. I'd want it to be something that gets people back to work, though, not just a cheque.

S2.say: I'd say it's going too fast because companies rushed, not because of the technology, and you don't throw a country's workers out in two years, so families need to pull together.
S2.think: If robots can build lines by 2028, my trade is finished before my son leaves school. Our savings and a two-thirds-paid house help, but the apprentices and I would have nowhere to go.
S2.do: Cancels the planned house extension and puts the money on the mortgage in the first month. Works out with his wife how long they'd last, asks his son to rethink college plans and starts selling firewood from their woodland.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, quiet at dinner in a way his wife would notice.
S2.quote: I'm supposed to be the one who knows. I'd tell them to save every penny and stick together, and I'd keep ringing round, but I wouldn't lie to them.
S2.fieldNote: His pro-business view bends here: he blames companies for rushing. Not having answers for his apprentices hurts him most. He'd accept public help for his children's sake but wants it tied to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for working people to get ready if the companies are honest about the plan. I'd want apprenticeships for the new jobs, not just courses on a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright. In five years I'd be forty-eight, the house nearly paid off, and the robot crews would need someone who knows how a line goes up to tell them when they've got it wrong. That could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep working, keep paying down the house. Once the first robot crews were working on someone else's job and I'd seen them, I'd do the training to supervise them. Keep the firewood going on the side, it's good exercise anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a robot crew enough to train on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one set a pole on a slope, in the rain, with a farmer shouting at it. If it can do that, it's real. If all I see is a video in a dry car park, I'll wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for your apprentices with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd have time to get into the robot side early, which they'd be better at than me. I'd push them to. I'd say, I'll teach you how a line should look, you learn how to make the machine do it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for workers to get ready if companies are honest about their plans, and I'd want apprenticeships for the new jobs rather than laptop courses.
S3.think: I'd be alright because at forty-eight the house would be nearly paid, and robot crews would need someone who knows how a line goes up to tell them when it's wrong.
S3.do: Keeps working and paying down the house, then trains to supervise robot crews once he's seen them working on other jobs. Keeps selling firewood on the side.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, sleeping fine most nights.
S3.quote: Seeing one set a pole on a slope, in the rain, with a farmer shouting at it. If it can do that, it's real.
S3.fieldNote: His trust test is practical and specific, which fits his steady approach to change. He imagines a split where he teaches standards and apprentices run the machines. Five years leaves him uneasy but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who's willing to work and learn will find their place. I'd say towns and companies should be setting up apprenticeships for whatever comes next, starting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm not too worried about ten years. I'd be fifty-three, the house would be paid, the kids would be grown. I'd have time to see what works, move onto the robot side, or just keep going till they don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building lines, keep training apprentices, and in a few years do the robot supervision training once it's proven. Help Daniel and Sofia choose their paths with their eyes open. Maybe turn the firewood into a bit more of a business for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit wistful, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you wistful about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Harold. He taught me, I teach them, and that chain might stop with my lot. That's the part I'd miss, not the work, the passing it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help Sofia choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's twelve and loves animals. I'd tell her to follow that, but to pick the part where you need a person, like the farm vet who comes out at night. I'd say it once, then leave it. She's stubborn like her mother.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and willing workers will find their place, and towns and companies should set up apprenticeships for whatever comes next.
S4.think: I'm not too worried about ten years, because at fifty-three the house would be paid and the children grown. I'd have time to move to the robot side or keep going until I'm not needed.
S4.do: Keeps building lines and training apprentices, then takes robot supervision training once it's proven. Helps his children choose paths with open eyes and considers growing the firewood sales into a small business.
S4.quote: He taught me, I teach them, and that chain might stop with my lot.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he's calm about money and work. What he'd mourn is the chain of passing skills from mentor to apprentice. He'd advise his children once, then step back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is the companies being made to pay for real apprenticeships into whatever new work there is, so young people learn from someone, not from a screen. And honesty about the timeline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who teaches the robots. Somebody's got to show them what a good job looks like. I'd want it to be people like Harold, not someone in an office who's never been up a pole.

headlineQuote: A man who's afraid of climbing should find another trade.
portrait: Erik Reyes is a 43-year-old line construction worker building new feeders out to solar farms, and he usually has two apprentices with him, passing on what his old mentor Harold taught him. He's married to Rosa, a part-time bookkeeper, with two children, a mostly paid-off house and good savings. He uses AI now and then on his phone and learns new tools once they're proven. He's calm in the mild scenarios and anxious with fast AGI, mostly because he'd have no answers for his apprentices. With five or ten years he plans to supervise robot crews, and what he'd miss most is passing the trade on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his trade could be finished before his son leaves school.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying for real apprenticeships into new work so young people learn from a person, plus honesty about the timeline.
